en: Preface to the Fifteenth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The Section on the Dhyānapāramitā,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery.
Ah, how vast is the function of the mind! When it is stirred, discordant competition arises;

when it is stilled, the myriad transformations nearly cease. On a grand scale, it fills the entire dharma-realm; on a minute scale, it enters even the subtlest atoms (*paramāṇu*). Thus, the oceans and mountains surrounding the regions are but reflections of the mind;
the physical form, eyes, and ears are but its manifestations.
The cycle of birth and death is the mind’s delusion;
Bodhi’s luminous vastness is the mind’s awakening.
Within the triple world there is nothing else; it is truly difficult to tame.
To regulate them in a single place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

Thus, one continues the excellent assembly of Anāthapiṇḍada and opens the wondrous gate of *samādhi*. This clarifies that when the category of concentration is perfected, the source of the mind is truly serene;
when both sinking and agitation are simultaneously rejected, both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are purified.

Dwelling in fellowship beyond the realm of desire, soaring solitary above the pinnacle of existence, the flames of objective phenomena are extinguished yet shine all the more brightly; the branches of causal conditions are pruned yet become even more solemn. Serene as all burdens are exhausted, movement accords with virtue.

Therefore, to unify them is the One Suchness; to weigh them is the Two Characteristics; to exhaust them is the Three Liberations; to rely upon them is the Four Divine Abidings; to practice them is the Five Seals; to examine them is the Six Mindfulnesses; to gather them is the Seven Good Dharmas; to flow through them is the Eight Emancipations; to ascend through them is the Nine Successive Stages; and to extend them is the Ten Pervasions.

As for the remaining categories such as the four foundations of mindfulness and the four immeasurables, as well as the five faculties and the five powers—none of them fail to span all stages of dhyāna, flourishing vibrantly within the fundamental states;
they are stored within the surging depths of samādhi, towering majestically at the ultimate limits.
It is like clay on a potter’s wheel or gold in a smithy; it exists solely for whatever purpose it may serve—how could there be any limitation?

Thus, they are capable of perfecting flavors and penetrating the subtle, wielding spiritual wonders with such swiftness that the sun and moon are eclipsed above and the rivers and mountains tremble below. Their bodies pervade the ten directions and their voices extend throughout the six realms of existence. They intermingle the natures of water and fire and transform the forms of metal and earth. Exhausting every path of transformation, they transcend the realm of thought and deliberation. Possessing subtle and wondrous meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not seek rebirth in superior states for their own gratification;
instead, they close the gates to the evil destinies and willingly endure the pains of hell for the sake of benefiting others.

There are also various divisions of the eight dhyānas and different names for samādhis, such as Sun-Turning Starlight, Moon-Love Flower-Virtue, Playful Agility, and Pure Illumination; numbering in the hundreds or thousands, they are difficult to ascend and difficult to master, yet all rely upon the power of exposition, which is fully set forth in these compiled texts.
In total, these have been compiled into two fascicles, and have not yet undergone a second translation.
As they enter deeply into the secrets of dhyāna, who would dare to abandon them!
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 509.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Part One of the Fifteenth Chapter on the Perfection of Dhyāna. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, by what skillful means should they abide in the perfection of meditative concentration?
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should first enter the first dhyāna.”
Having entered this first dhyāna, one should reflect:

"Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly entered such meditative absorption, performed what was to be done, and attained tranquility of body and mind; therefore, this dhyāna has been beneficial to me.
Now I shall enter it once more to perform what is to be done, for this is the foundation of all meritorious qualities."
Next, one should enter the second dhyāna.
Having entered this second dhyāna, one should reflect:

"Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly entered such meditative absorption; it has performed what was to be done for me, bringing tranquility to my body and mind, and therefore this dhyāna has been beneficial to me."
"Now I should enter again and perform what is to be done; this is the basis for all meritorious qualities.
Next, one should enter the third dhyāna.
Having entered this third dhyāna, one should form this thought:

"Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly entered such meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and performed what was to be done; because my body and mind were tranquil therein, this meditative absorption has been beneficial to me.
Now I shall enter it once more to perform what is to be done, for this is the basis of all meritorious qualities."
Next, one should enter the fourth dhyāna.
Having entered this fourth dhyāna, one should form this thought:
"Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly entered such a dhyāna and performed what was to be done; because my body and mind were tranquil therein, this dhyāna has been a benefactor to me."
"Now one should enter once more and perform what is to be done; this is the basis for all merit.
Having thus entered these four dhyānas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should further reflect:

"These four dhyānas possess great beneficence toward the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas and serve as their support. That is to say, when the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas is about to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they all gradually enter these four dhyānas. Having entered these four dhyānas, they rely upon the fourth dhyāna to manifest the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), subdue the armies of Māra, and achieve unsurpassed awakening."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"In the past, all the assemblies of bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivated the perfection of meditative concentration; I, too, should cultivate it.
In the past, all the assemblies of bodhisattva mahāsattvas studied the perfection of meditative concentration; I, too, should study it."

"In the past, the assemblies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas all relied upon the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) to evoke the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) according to their inclinations; I, too, should rely upon this perfection of meditative concentration to evoke the perfection of wisdom according to my inclinations."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not rely upon the fourth dhyāna to skillfully enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), realize suchness (*tathatā*), and abandon the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

There are no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not rely upon the fourth dhyāna to skillfully evoke the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), and realize the wisdom of a Tathāgata. Therefore, you should know that the fourth dhyāna possesses great merit for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it enables them to initially enter the state of right determination, realize suchness, and abandon the nature of an ordinary being, and finally to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."

For this reason, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should frequently manifest entry into the fourth dhyāna; yet, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to manifest entry into these four dhyānas, they do not relish or become attached to the bliss of the four dhyānas nor to the superior and sublime states of rebirth that flow from them.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these four kinds of meditative concentrations (dhyāna) as a supreme skillful means to attract all meritorious qualities."

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying upon the fourth dhyāna, gives rise to the perception of the sphere of infinite space and induces the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying upon the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space, gives rise to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness and induces the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying on the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, gives rise to the perception of the sphere of nothingness and draws forth the concentration of the sphere of nothingness.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying on the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, gives rise to the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and draws forth the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In this way, although the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is able to manifest entry into the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they do not relish or become attached to these four formless attainments nor to the superior and sublime states of birth obtained thereby.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though able to manifest entry into the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, not actually enter it?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fear falling into the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not manifest entry into the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). They must not become attached to the tranquil bliss of this meditative absorption, thereby delighting in the realization of the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood and entering parinirvāṇa.”

"When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate this meaning, although they are able to manifest entry into the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they do not actually enter it.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do; for although they manifest entry into such concentrations, they do not give rise to attachment toward those concentrations. Furthermore, although they manifest entry into such concentrations and are able to give rise to superior functions, they do not depart from freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*)."
The Buddha said: "So it is!
It is just as you have said."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and are able to perform what is difficult to do.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are most exceedingly rare; that is to say, although they manifest entry into the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions—states of tranquil bliss—they neither relish them nor are they separated from their freedom from defilement.

I shall now briefly provide you with an analogy to bring about a complete understanding of this meaning. Suppose there were a person born in this Jambudvīpa who, though not yet free from the defilements of the desire realm, might travel to Uttarakuru.

There, they would see that the women of that continent are unattached, beautiful in form, and enjoy themselves with ease; they would see that the clothing and ornaments there are fresh, pure, and exquisite, all growing spontaneously from trees; they would see that there is fragrant non-glutinous rice, sweet and delicious, which grows of itself without being sown; and they would see that everywhere on that continent there are various kinds of rare treasures, most delightful to behold. Seeing that the people of that continent enjoy such things as they please, without fixed attachment, and that while enjoying them they do not become excessively infatuated, but having enjoyed them, they cast them aside without longing—[this is the analogy].

Although the people of Jambudvīpa have not yet abandoned their defilements, they behold those various sublime things and, without becoming attached to them, relinquish them and return; one should know that such persons are truly rare.
"In this way, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest entry into the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions—
experiencing their tranquility and bliss, and observing the various subtle, tranquil, and sublime merits arising therein—
they do not relish them or become attached; instead, they return to the desire realm through skillful means based on desire."
Regarding the constituents of the elements, they diligently cultivate and study the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
they diligently cultivate and study internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness.
Through the contemplation of ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness,

self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they diligently cultivate and study all dharmas.
One contemplates true suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),

non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),

the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm. With diligent application in study, one [contemplates] that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises;

conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, becoming arises; conditioned by becoming, birth arises; conditioned by birth, old age and death arise.

Contemplating this, one diligently practices and trains so that with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness...

Thus one contemplates: with the cessation of name-and-form, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases;
with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease.
He diligently trains in the contemplation of the noble truth of suffering as suffering, as impermanent, as empty, and as non-self;
he diligently trains in the contemplation of the noble truth of the origin as cause, as origination, as birth, and as condition;
he diligently trains in the contemplation of the noble truth of cessation as cessation, as peace, as sublime, and as renunciation.
One diligently practices and trains in the noble truth of the contemplation of the path, suchness, practice, and the way out;
one diligently practices and trains in the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and one diligently practices and trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
They diligently train in the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the noble path;
they diligently train in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases;

they diligently train in the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they diligently train in the stage of pure observation, the stage of the spiritual lineage, and the eighth stage.

The knowledge of the stage of the ground, the stage of one who has seen the truths, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha,
the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata; and the diligent cultivation and study of the stage of extreme joy,
the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of blazing wisdom, the stage of extreme difficulty to conquer, the stage of presence, and the stage of remoteness.
The Ground of Action, the Immovable Ground, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
they diligently train in the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; they diligently train in the purification of the five eyes and the six supreme supernormal powers;
and they diligently train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges.
Understanding, he diligently cultivates and studies great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
he diligently cultivates and studies the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
he diligently cultivates and studies the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; he diligently cultivates and studies the one...
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

they diligently train in the analytical skillful knowledge of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*);
they diligently train in all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and they diligently train in the [qualities] of all Buddhas.
"Even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, as well as the exhortation of sentient beings to cultivate all wholesome dharmas—
such matters are truly rare.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas permit the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to relinquish the tranquil bliss of the superior meditative stages and instead receive inferior bodies within the desire realm?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"It is the natural law of all Buddhas that they do not permit bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be born in the long-lived heavens."

Why is this? Śāriputra, let it not be that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are born in the long-lived heavens, thereby becoming remote from the cultivation of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the other boundless factors conducive to enlightenment; for by such means, they would be delayed in realizing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha permits the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to relinquish the tranquil bliss of the superior meditative stages and instead take on inferior bodies in the desire realm; however, he does not permit the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be born in the long-lived heavens and thereby lose their original vows.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The bodhisattva mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do; namely, they relinquish the supreme meditative concentration, tranquility, and bliss, and instead take on a body in an inferior, defiled realm.”

For example, suppose there is a person who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire. While wandering in a forest, he encounters a woman of exquisite beauty whose form and features are so lovely as to be deeply pleasing; although he observes her various limbs in detail, he is able to restrain his mind and does not succumb to negligence.
Later, in another place, he encounters a woman whose appearance is coarse, ugly, loathsome, and lowly, yet he instead gives rise to greedy attachment and consequently falls into negligence.

Thus, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas frequently abide in the four sublime and tranquil meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they are able to relinquish them and instead take on various defiled, inferior bodies within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, they are most rare and capable of performing what is difficult to do.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas relinquishes the superior stages to assume a body within the desire realm, you should know that this constitutes skillful means.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,

these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, diligently seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, relinquish their bodies in the superior realms and are reborn in the desire realm, giving rise to superior mental attention and skillful means.

"Although one observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence in the aggregate of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence in the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

Although they observe that within the aggregate of form there is neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure, and likewise observe that within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) neither self nor non-self can be found, and likewise observe that within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, vijñāna-skandha) neither self nor non-self can be found, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the aggregate of form is entirely unattainable, and likewise observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unattainable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of emptiness or non-emptiness of the aggregate of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of emptiness or non-emptiness of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of both the characterized and the uncharacterized within the aggregate of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration within the aggregate of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all aspects (sarvajñajñāna).

Although one observes that the nature of the aggregate of form—whether it is detached or non-detached—is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observes that the nature of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable as being either detached or non-detached, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of both tranquility and non-tranquility cannot be found within the aggregate of form, and likewise observe that the nature of both tranquility and non-tranquility cannot be found within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Although one observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence is entirely unapprehendable in the sense-base of the eye, and likewise observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence is unapprehendable in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

Although they contemplate the eye-faculty and find that neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure can be apprehended, and although they contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-faculties and likewise find that neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure can be apprehended, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Although they observe that within the sense-base of the eye, neither a self nor a non-self can be found, and likewise observe that within the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, neither a self nor a non-self can be found, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the sense-sphere of the eye is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the sense-spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the emptiness or non-emptiness of the sense base of the eye is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the emptiness or non-emptiness of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they contemplate that the nature of the eye-base, being both with and without marks, is entirely unapprehendable, and although they contemplate that the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, being both with and without marks, is likewise unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they contemplate the sense bases of the eye, and find that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration is entirely unattainable, and although they contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, finding that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration therein is likewise unattainable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

Although they observe that the nature of the eye-base being either detached or non-detached is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases being either detached or non-detached is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all aspects.

Although one observes that the nature of the eye-base, whether quiescent or non-quiescent, is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observes that the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, whether quiescent or non-quiescent, is also unapprehendable, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Although one observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence is entirely unapprehendable in the sphere of form, and likewise observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence is also unapprehendable in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes."

Although they contemplate the sphere of forms and find that neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure can be apprehended, and although they contemplate the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena and likewise find that neither pleasure nor the nature of pleasure can be apprehended, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

Although they observe that in the sphere of forms the nature of self and non-self is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that in the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena the nature of self and non-self is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

Although they observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the sphere of form is entirely unattainable, and likewise observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also unattainable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding the sphere of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

Although they observe that the characteristics of the sense-base of form, as well as its nature of being without characteristics, are entirely unapprehendable—and although they observe that the characteristics of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, as well as their nature of being without characteristics, are likewise unapprehendable—they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they contemplate that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration in the sense-base of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise contemplate that the nature of aspiration and non-aspiration in the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

Although they observe that the nature of detachment or non-detachment in the sense-sphere of form is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of detachment or non-detachment in the sense-spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of tranquility and non-tranquility in the sphere of form is entirely unapprehendable, and although they observe that the nature of tranquility and non-tranquility in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is likewise unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes.

"Although one observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence in the eye-element is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observes that the nature of permanence and impermanence in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is also unapprehendable, one does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

Although they contemplate that within the eye-element there is no pleasure and its nature of pleasure is entirely unattainable, and although they contemplate that within the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements there is likewise no pleasure and their nature of pleasure is unattainable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of self and non-self in the eye-element is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of self and non-self in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although they observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the eye-element is entirely unapprehendable, and likewise observe that the nature of purity and impurity in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is also unapprehendable, they do not abandon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Śāriputra said:

Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not permit the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to attachment toward the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, nor to dwell therein for long.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If one is born in the desire realm, one can swiftly bring the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) to full completion; those born in the form or formless realms lack such capacity.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"The assembly of bodhisattvas is truly rare and performs what is difficult to do; for these bodhisattvas, having dwelt in supreme meditative concentration, nevertheless relinquish it to receive inferior dharmas."
It is, for example, like a person who encounters a hidden treasure and, though grasping precious jewels in his hand, casts them away;
yet at a later time, seeing cowrie shells and pearls, he reaches out to seize them and carries them into his house.
In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enters the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, dwelling in peace and bliss as they please;

yet later, they relinquish these states and are reborn in the desire realm, assuming various inferior bodies and minds, and relying upon them to practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other boundless factors conducive to enlightenment.

The Buddha, contemplating this meaning, should permit that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas be born in the long-lived heavens, where they may practice for a long duration the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other boundless factors conducive to enlightenment; by means of this, they will swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas are born in the long-lived heavens, they will be unable to cultivate such meritorious qualities and will not be able to swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas enter the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, which are tranquil and blissful, these bodhisattvas do not form this thought:

Nor do they think:
"By means of the dhyānas and the formless attainments, I transcend the realm of form and the formless realm.

These bodhisattvas enter the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments for the sake of tranquil bliss, solely desiring to manifest sovereign supernormal powers to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, and also wishing to subdue their coarse and heavy body and mind so that it becomes capable of cultivating all meritorious qualities.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter various supreme concentrations that are tranquil and blissful; through their skill in means, they take on bodies in the desire realm without ever falling away from those supreme concentrations.

Therefore, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas neither transcends the triple world nor is stained by attachment; through skillful means, they assume bodies in the desire realm to benefit sentient beings, draw near to the Buddhas, and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha said: "So it is!
It is just as you have said."
The omniscient wisdom attained by the Tathāgata transcends the three realms and is not subsumed within them.
