In this way, bodhisattva mahāsattvas abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration encompass the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā)."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), take up the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā)?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

“If bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate and perfect great loving-kindness and great compassion, desiring to bring benefit to all sentient beings, they abide in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā). Even when encountering adverse conditions, their minds remain free from defilement. In this way, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who abide in the perfection of meditative concentration embrace the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).”
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, while dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

"If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) and does not give rise to attachment toward the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, then these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration embrace the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of generosity?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

"If the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), gives rise to thoughts of great compassion toward all sentient beings, vows never to abandon any sentient being, and seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in order to bring them liberation from the suffering of birth and death, they should form this thought:

'I shall certainly gather in sentient beings through the gift of the Great Dharma, and I shall constantly proclaim for the sake of sentient beings the essential points of the truly pure Dharma that forever sever all afflictions.'"
“In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, embraces the perfection of generosity.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, by what name should this bodhisattva mahāsattva be known?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as a non-retrogressive bodhisattva.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do; having already dwelt within such supreme meditative concentrations in tranquil bliss, they are further able to relinquish them and again accept inferior dharmas associated with the desire realm, benefiting sentient beings through their skillful means."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do.
You should know that these bodhisattvas, in order to deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, don the firm armor of great vows and constantly maintain this thought:
"I shall deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.

I shall ensure that the Buddha’s pure Dharma-eye is never interrupted, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings; yet while performing these deeds, I shall remain without attachment, realizing that there is no sentient being who attains nirvana, nor any who attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? All phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self.
When various sufferings arise, it is only suffering that arises; there is no agent who causes them to arise.
"When all sufferings are extinguished, there is only the extinction of suffering, and no one who can extinguish it.
You should know that likewise there is no one who can realize or attain the dharma of purity.
For this reason, you should know that the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is most rare and is able to perform what is difficult to do.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
You should know that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is most rare, for they are able to perform what is difficult."

Why is this? Although, in reality, there are no phenomena that arise or cease, nor enter parinirvāṇa, nor realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, yet the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practices all bodhisattva deeds in order to deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. They seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, desiring to proclaim to sentient beings the dharmas that eternally sever greed, hatred, and delusion, so that they may diligently practice and study to attain parinirvāṇa;
or they proclaim to sentient beings the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, so that they may diligently practice and study to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is undistracted and remains continuously established in mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who dwells in the perfection of meditative concentration."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in mental attention associated with the stage of a śrāvaka or mental attention associated with the stage of a pratyekabuddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one whose mind is constantly distracted.
Why is this so, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and trains in mental orientations associated with the two vehicles, it creates an obstacle to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, causing the mind of enlightenment to remain constantly distracted.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may take as objects form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and tangibles, and give rise to various improper mental attentions that disturb their minds of generosity and so forth, these do not obstruct the bodhisattvas' pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).”

If a phenomenon cannot obstruct a bodhisattva’s knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), even though it manifests before them, one should know that it is not called a phenomenon that is utterly contrary to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; nor does it constitute a permanent falling away from the bodhisattva’s stage of meditative absorption (samādhibhūmi).
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas praise the merits possessed by the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, yet do not praise the śrāvakas?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?”
“Can a firefly perform the function of illumination for the people of this Jambudvīpa that the sun performs?
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra replied, “No!”
"World-Honored One! No, indeed! Sugata!"
The Buddha said: "So it is!
It is just as you have said."
"The tasks that all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to accomplish are likewise such that they cannot be achieved by any śrāvakas.
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should one understand that it is only the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can form this thought?"
"I shall deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder;
I shall ensure that the Buddha’s pure Dharma-eye remains uninterrupted and unceasing, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
"How should one understand that it is only the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can perform such sublime deeds, and not the śrāvakas?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Do you now observe within this assembly of śrāvakas a single bhikṣu who is able to form such thoughts and accomplish such tasks as the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does?"
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said: “No,
World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! As I now observe this assembly of śrāvakas,
there is not a single bhikṣu who can conceive such a thought as these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do, nor is there anyone capable of accomplishing such a deed."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha praises only the bodhisattvas and does not praise the śrāvakas."

Observe that among this assembly, none of the arhats have such thoughts, nor can they accomplish such deeds; one should know that no followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle possess the capacity for the deeds performed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Therefore, I have said:
"For example, just as the solar disc performs the function of providing illumination for Jambudvīpa, a firefly cannot accomplish this.

That is to say, the solar disc emits immeasurable light, universally illuminating all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, whereas the light of a firefly illuminates only its own body and nothing else.

In this way, the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas subdues their own afflictions and evil karma, and is also able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to leave behind all afflictions and evil karma and enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, or to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;

whereas those of the Śrāvaka vehicle can only subdue the afflictions and evil karma within themselves and cannot benefit immeasurable sentient beings. Therefore, the activities of the Śrāvakas are not as entirely superior as those of the Bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is like a skilled archer who has applied himself to his training; his hands, body, bow, and weapons are all well-disciplined, and having mastered all martial arts, he has reached the ultimate perfection, having received the king’s stipend for a hundred thousand years."

When the king is about to engage in battle with an enemy, he entrusts the elephant and cavalry forces, as well as all weapons and armaments, to him for command, hoping to utterly destroy the wicked foe without any loss.

Thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having already resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and having already cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, have attained skillfulness in subduing the conduct of greed, hatred, and delusion among all classes of sentient beings.

For this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha specifically praises the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, instructing and exhorting them to practice diligently so that they may correctly bring forth the provisions for enlightenment, swiftly fulfill their great vows, and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, thereby teaching all sentient beings the essential points of the pure Dharma that can forever sever greed, hatred, and delusion.

Therefore, the deeds performed by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas while donning their armor are such that neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas can perform them; for this reason, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas praise and encourage bodhisattvas, but not śrāvakas.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it should be known that whatever the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do, there is no state of mind that is not concentrated. That is to say, when the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), it should be known that at that time their minds are also in a state of concentration;”
If one abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, it should be known that at that time the mind is also in meditative concentration;
if one abides in the perfection of patience, it should be known that at that time the mind is also in meditative concentration;
if one abides in the perfection of diligence, it should be known that at that time the mind is also in meditative concentration.
If one abides in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), it should be known that at that time the mind is also in samādhi;
if one abides in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it should be known that at that time the mind is also in samādhi;
if one abides in any other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), it should be known that at that time the mind is also in samādhi.

Just as wherever vaidūrya is located, it never abandons its own precious color—whether it is in a golden vessel, a silver vessel, a crystal vessel, or one made of copper, iron, or clay—it always does not abandon the color of vaidūrya;

so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom, or abide in any other factors conducive to enlightenment, you should know that at those times their minds are constantly in samādhi. This is how I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught.
At that time, the Buddha praised Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"So it is! So it is! Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, fully abide in the first dhyāna.

Having thus dwelled in the first dhyāna, if one takes pleasure in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, one should be known as a bodhisattva with a distracted mind; it should be known that such a person dwells in a state of mind that is not in meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, attain internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, and abide fully in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss."

Having thus dwelled in this second dhyāna, if one takes pleasure in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, one should know that such a bodhisattva has a distracted mind; one should know that they abide in a state of mind that is not in meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having detached from joy, abide in equanimity, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing bodily bliss—of which the noble ones say, 'He dwells happily, possessing mindfulness and equanimity'—they fully abide in the third dhyāna."

Having thus dwelt in this third dhyāna, if one takes pleasure in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, one should know that such a bodhisattva has a distracted mind; one should know that they abide in a state of mind that is not fixed in samādhi.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abandons pleasure and abandons pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

Having thus dwelled in this fourth dhyāna, if one takes pleasure in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, one should know that this is called a distracted bodhisattva; one should know that such a person dwells with a mind not established in meditative concentration.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To what extent should one know that a bodhisattva’s mind is concentrated?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"Whenever bodhisattva mahāsattvas encounter various sentient beings, they should form this thought:

'I shall diligently cultivate the bodhisattva practices so that, when I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I will certainly cause those classes of sentient beings to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, or to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete bodhi.'"
Up to this point, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the three refuges, and those sentient beings, having established themselves in the three refuges, dedicate the roots of virtue thus accumulated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—up to this point, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the five precepts, and those sentient beings, having established themselves in the five precepts, dedicate the roots of goodness thus accumulated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the eight precepts, and those sentient beings, having dwelled in the eight precepts, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), by this one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the ten precepts, and those sentient beings, having established themselves in the ten precepts, dedicate the roots of goodness thus accumulated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), by this one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to undertake and maintain the ten paths of wholesome action, and those sentient beings, having established themselves in the ten paths of wholesome action, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the complete precepts, and those sentient beings, having come to abide in the complete precepts, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the mind of a bodhisattva is fixed."
“Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhorts sentient beings to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts, and those sentient beings, having established themselves in the bodhisattva precepts, dedicate the roots of goodness thus accumulated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be understood that, up to this point, the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the perfection of generosity, and those sons and daughters of good family, having become established in the perfection of generosity, take these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes—by this, one should know that the mind of a bodhisattva is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and those good sons and good daughters, having become established in the perfection of ethical discipline, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), it should be understood that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), and those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves in the perfection of patience, take these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—to this extent, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the perfection of diligence, and those good sons and good daughters, having established themselves in the perfection of diligence, take these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that up to this point the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), and those good sons and good daughters, having become established in the perfection of meditative concentration, take these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—to this extent, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and those good sons and good daughters, having become established in the perfection of wisdom, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna)—to this extent, one should know that the mind of the bodhisattva is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort good sons and good daughters to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and if those good sons and good daughters, having established themselves therein, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be understood that the bodhisattva’s mind is thus stabilized."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide sons of good family and daughters of good family to practice the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, and if those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be understood that up to this point the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort various sons and daughters of good family to practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, and if those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort various sons and daughters of good family to practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and once those sons and daughters of good family have become established therein, they take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes; up to this point, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, and those good sons and good daughters, having become established therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the stage of pure observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), the stage of lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of possessing vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of attenuation (*tanū-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), the stage of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*), the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*), and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*); and if those good sons and good daughters, having become established therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), it should be known that up to this point the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Blazing Wisdom Stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Dharma-Cloud Stage; once those sons and daughters of good family have settled therein, they take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes. Up to this point, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and those good sons and good daughters, having become established therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that up to this point the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas use skillful means to exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and four analytical knowledges, and those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes—by this one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and if those good sons and good daughters, having become established therein, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), one should know that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the dharma of non-forgetfulness and to abide constantly in equanimity, and if those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that by this measure the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
“Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and if those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take the roots of virtue thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*), by this one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to practice for the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and if those good sons and good daughters, having established themselves therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), then by this measure one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take these accumulated roots of goodness and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be understood that the bodhisattva's mind is thus fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide various sons and daughters of good family to practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, and those sons and daughters of good family, having established themselves therein, take the roots of goodness thus accumulated and dedicate them toward seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), by this one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully exhort and guide good sons and good daughters to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings, and once those good sons and good daughters have established themselves therein, they take the roots of virtue thus accumulated and dedicate them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—to this extent, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is fixed."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with a profound mind, rejoice in the virtues such as generosity practiced by others, and dedicate [the merit] toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it should be known that, to this extent, the bodhisattva’s mind is concentrated."

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has attained concentration of mind in all circumstances, it should be known that they are said to be dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never remain apart from the superior mental engagement with the knowledge of all modes.

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas never depart from the supreme mental engagement of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*), they should be known as dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). Thus, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, manifest boundless and sublime qualities and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"It should be known that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, abiding immovably in the fourth dhyāna, relinquishes the formations of life and manifests entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder."

Therefore, the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) possesses great benefaction for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Therefore, among all other meditative concentrations—with the exception of the concentration of the Tathāgata—the dhyāna-pāramitā in which the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, and the unsurpassed.
Why is this so? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

The bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) is never separated from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), whereas the meditative concentration of the followers of the two vehicles is definitively separated from such mental engagement. Therefore, compared to the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration, theirs is inferior; the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration is superior to theirs.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If all śrāvakas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka;
likewise, if bodhisattvas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena, become free from all attachments, and attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

How can it be said that the meditative concentration of a śrāvaka is definitively separated from mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), whereas the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is never separated from mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?"
When the śrāvakas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka;

likewise, when the bodhisattvas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena, become free from all attachments, and attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Would those śrāvakas be called Tathāgatas?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“I shall provide you with another parable; by means of this parable, those who possess wisdom will easily understand the profound meaning.”
“Suppose an ordinary person were to suddenly ascend the royal throne; would that person then be called a king?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, “No!”
World-Honored One! Why is this?
It is because that person lacks merit and lacks the marks of a king.
The Buddha said:

“In this way, although these śrāvakas are able to manifest entry into the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka, they lack the Tathāgata’s superior qualities such as the powers and fearlessnesses, as well as the marks and signs of excellence; thus they are not called Tathāgatas, because they remain far removed from the mental engagement associated with omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).”
Because they lack the qualities of a Buddha, they are called śrāvakas.
Otherwise, why would they not be called Buddhas?
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

The meditative concentrations (dhyāna) in which the śrāvakas abide are inferior in nature because they lack superior qualities; compared to the meditative concentrations in which bodhisattvas abide, they do not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

A bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration is never separated from the knowledge of all modes; it purifies buddha-fields, brings sentient beings to maturity, and brings forth boundless, sublime qualities.
"Because of this, the sublime concentration in which the bodhisattva abides cannot be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called the sublime concentration of a bodhisattva?"
"What is the name of this supreme concentration?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"The supreme concentration of a bodhisattva is named 'Inconceivable' (acintya)."
For what reason?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The power of such a supreme concentration is inconceivable, for it enables one to swiftly realize all-knowledge.
This supreme concentration is also called "benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings in the world.
Why is this so? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, enter this meditative concentration through skillful means.

When such a supreme concentration manifests, it can induce boundless, subtle, and sublime concentrations, leading them swiftly to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and to perform great benefit for all sentient beings.

When such a supreme concentration manifests, it induces boundless skillful means, whereby they instruct and teach immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to induce untainted *dhyāna*, realize the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), sever all afflictions, and enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, or to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

For this reason, the sublime meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is also called "benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings in the world. Therefore, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should train in the perfection of meditative concentration;
if they train in the perfection of meditative concentration, they will swiftly be able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I maintain that the various concentrations attained by śrāvakas are superior to the concentrations of bodhisattvas."

Why is this? Because the śrāvakas fully attain the nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), whereas the bodhisattvas among them attain only the first eight. Since the bodhisattvas do not attain the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti), the concentration of the śrāvakas is superior to that of the bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“A bodhisattva also attains the cessation of perception and feeling; that is to say, although they have already attained mastery over this samādhi, they do not manifest its entry.”

Why is this? The Tathāgata does not permit the assembly of bodhisattvas to manifest entry into this samādhi, lest by manifesting such entry they should fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
I shall provide you with another simile; for those who possess wisdom can easily understand profound meanings by means of similes."
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, though he has attained mastery over all the minor kingdoms and towns in the borderlands, does not personally travel to those lands and towns—
does this mean that because the wheel-turning monarch does not go there, he lacks mastery over those places?

In this way, although the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not actually enter the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, they have already attained mastery over this absorption; by virtue of this mastery, it is said that they have "attained" it.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is not that all bodhisattvas never manifest entry into the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; rather, until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not permit them to manifest such entry.
However, once they have attained the sublime seat of awakening, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, also permit them to manifest entry."
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is not because bodhisattvas would fall into the stage of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas by entering this samādhi, nor because they might claim that the Buddhas are equal to the two vehicles, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not permit its manifestation.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration of coronation wishes to enter a marketplace to drink the wine of commoners.
At that time, a wise minister would admonish the great king, saying:"
"At this time and place, Your Majesty should not drink.
If you must drink, wait until you have reached the palace.
What do you think?
"Does the King not have the power to drink the wine in the marketplace?

Yet that wise minister earnestly admonishes and remonstrates so as not to let the King drink. However, for a Kṣatriya consecrated Great King, it is contrary to the Dharma to drink at an improper place or time; although he should not drink, he possesses full mastery over all things such as wine in the marketplace."
Why is this? Because the king possesses sovereign mastery over all persons and things within every kingdom and city. Likewise, a bodhisattva possesses superior wisdom;

by virtue of this wisdom, he is able to repeatedly manifest entry into the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), yet he does not manifest such entry because the Buddha has not permitted it.

Why is this? If a bodhisattva were to enter the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*) prematurely, it would be neither the proper time nor the proper place.

Only when the bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), permanently destroying all perceptions of false appearances and realizing the realm of ambrosia (*amṛtadhātu*), does he then enter the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception. Subsequently, having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*), he turns the sublime wheel of Dharma, endowed with the thirty-two marks, to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and marvelous; they are able to perform what is difficult to do, in that although they possess the power to realize the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, they do not personally realize the exhaustion of outflows for the sake of sentient beings.”

Why is this? Because for all bodhisattvas, throughout the long night, they contemplate the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and their superior intention (adhyāśaya) is constantly present before them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
These bodhisattvas, throughout the long night, contemplate the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and their superior intention (adhyāśaya) is ever present before them.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
These bodhisattvas, contemplating this benefit, are able to enter the nine successive meditative attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), yet they do not fully enter them. Why is this? "
These bodhisattvas possess skillful means; although they have attained mastery over all meditative concentrations, they are able to refrain from entering them.

Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, whether they have first resolved their minds for awakening or have already reached the stage of non-retrogression, all bodhisattvas should abide in this perfection of meditative concentration.
If bodhisattvas can constantly abide in such perfection of meditative concentration, they will be able to bring benefit to all sentient beings and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“It should be known that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possesses great power; they are able to perform beneficial deeds for sentient beings, and they are also able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha said: “So it is!
It is just as you have said.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of meditative concentration?”
"How does one employ skillful means to emerge from meditative concentration?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, free from desire and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained examination, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enter the first dhyāna; they proceed in this manner up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwelling fully therein. Regarding the form and formless realms, the dhyānas, and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), they practice them in forward and reverse order, as well as by leaping over stages, becoming thoroughly proficient and skilled, playing with them with sovereign ease, and then re-entering the non-concentrated mind of the desire realm."
Why is this? It is so that one does not give rise to the long-lived deities of the form and formless realms through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, it is so that one does not induce the mind of rebirth in those planes through the dhyānas and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the form and formless realms; rather, to prevent that mind from arising, one returns to the non-equipoised mind of the desire realm.

By giving rise to this mind, one returns to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thereby eliciting the boundless factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
beings born in the form (*rūpadhātu*) and formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack such capacity, because the bodies and minds of those born in the two higher realms are dull.

By means of this bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), having first cultivated the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) until they are thoroughly matured, he subsequently gives rise to a lower state of mind and returns to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). There, he accumulates the immeasurable provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*), and once these are perfected, he transcends the three realms (*traidhātuka*) and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"It is like a person who thinks to himself:
'By what means can I gain entry into the royal palace so that I may secretly sport with the king’s queens and concubines without the king’s knowledge, thereby preserving my life?'"

Having formed this thought, he sought various excellent medicines and took them so that his male form would either disappear or appear. Having obtained these medicines, he used skillful means to attend upon the king.
Once the king recognized him, he took the medicine for invisibility and then addressed the king, saying:
"I am now without form; I request to serve Your Majesty by guarding the harem."
The king ordered an investigation and then entrusted him with the affairs of the inner palace.
At that time, the man entered the royal harem and engaged in unrestrained sexual relations with the various consorts and ladies.
As one, two, or three months passed, fearing that the king might discover his conduct and cost him his life, he took a purgative and said to the king: [...the remainder of the passage...]
"I now suddenly manifest my male form once more; from this day forth, I request not to enter the inner palace.
At that time, the king praised him, saying:
"This is truly a virtuous man; he is able to advance and retreat of his own accord without contravening my law."
He is granted high rank and emoluments and entrusted with external affairs.
One should know that this person, through skillful means, is able to fulfill his own wishes, preserve his life, and furthermore receive the king’s generous bestowal of wealth and status.

Thus, through skillful means, the bodhisattva enters the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments; having attained mastery by successively transcending them, they again give rise to a lower state of mind and return to the desire realm. There, they draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and bring forth the boundless factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), until—without yet being fulfilled—they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because these bodhisattvas possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and do not abandon the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of all sentient beings. Thus, through their skillful means, these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), yet they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nor do they manifest entry into the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Until the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisaṃbhāra*) are fulfilled, they take on bodies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold the perfection of meditative concentration studied by the assembly of bodhisattvas; do not allow it to be forgotten or lost!"
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
“I have already received and upheld the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) studied by the assembly of bodhisattvas; I shall certainly never forget it!

At that time, when the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the other śrāvakas, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the entire great multitude—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Ninety-two.
